title: Celebrity Pharmacology

jokes.text: Flying a little low? Maybe you should get high.
jokes.setup: Buzby the bee character says he's tired from flying low
jokes.punchline: Pierce's character suggests he 'get high' — a double entendre bridging bee flight and drug use
jokes.explanation: Clean double entendre that works within the anti-drug play's logic — the bee/drug metaphor was designed for this pun. Economical and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Buzzby
dialogue.line: I'm exhausted, I can barely fly.

dialogue.speaker: Bumbleton
dialogue.line: You should get high!

dialogue.speaker: Buzzby
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Bumbleton
dialogue.line: You know, altitude. Get some air.

dialogue.speaker: Drugs
dialogue.line: Did someone say get high?

jokes.text: Drugs are like special honey. They give you a buzzzz.
jokes.setup: Pierce is playing 'Drugs' in a children's anti-drug show
jokes.punchline: He delivers a line that makes drugs sound appealing using bee/honey metaphor, 'buzz' being both a bee sound and a drug high
jokes.explanation: Extends the bee pun chain but also foreshadows the irony of an anti-drug character making drugs sound good — the seed of the episode's central joke.

dialogue.speaker: Drugs
dialogue.line: You know, I'm like a bee. I come in, I give you a buzz, and I leave you with something sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So you're saying you're going to call me honey?

jokes.text: Don't call me honey, honey.
jokes.setup: Pierce is supposed to have no lines as the character Drugs; he improvises
jokes.punchline: His improvised line is a sassy bee pun that he's clearly proud of — wrong tone for an anti-drug show, delivered with self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical, thoroughly Pierce: a character with no lines invents a line that's simultaneously a wordplay pun and deeply wrong for the show's message. The sass is completely in Pierce's oblivious register. Becomes a callback later.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Hey Drugs, you're looking pretty good today.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not even a character! You're just saying random words!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, Drugs seems to think I'm hilarious.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Drugs isn't a person, Pierce!

jokes.text: Pierce, Drugs doesn't say that. / You know, I don't say anything, by the way.
jokes.setup: Annie scolds Pierce for improvising as Drugs; Pierce defends himself
jokes.punchline: Pierce's self-defense ('I don't say anything') inadvertently proves Annie's point while missing it entirely
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce obliviousness — he cites his lack of lines as a defense while having just spoken the lines. Good character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, how is anyone supposed to know I'm the villain if I don't say anything?

jokes.text: Who's gonna be aware of a character that has no lines?
jokes.setup: Pierce complains that his character (Drugs) has no dialogue in the drug awareness show
jokes.punchline: He frames his ego trip as a logical argument about the show's effectiveness — missing the entire point that Drugs is supposed to be silent/villainous
jokes.explanation: Genuinely good Pierce logic — he's not entirely wrong (silent antagonists are hard to dramatize) but his motivation is pure ego, which makes the semi-valid argument funnier. Character-integrated and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying marijuana makes you work faster? That doesn't make sense. Wasn't there that whole Scooby-Doo thing where they were always eating snacks and solving mysteries really slowly?

jokes.text: Also, I noticed on page 15 I get flushed down a toilet. Consider yourself lucky.
jokes.setup: Pierce complains about his character being flushed down a toilet in the show
jokes.punchline: Jeff deadpans 'Consider yourself lucky' — the toilet disposal is apparently better than what Jeff faces
jokes.explanation: Jeff's dismissive deadpan is pitch-perfect, implying his own role is worse without elaborating. Economy of expression from Jeff is always a strength.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, I've been wearing my costume backwards this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That explains why I've felt so confident today. I thought it was the spray tan.

jokes.text: Does marijuana help people work faster? I thought it made them custom-paint their vans and solve mysteries.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if marijuana helps productivity
jokes.punchline: Jeff's reference to van-painting and mystery-solving — Scooby-Doo stoner joke delivered as a sincere counterpoint
jokes.explanation: Smart pop-culture reference that works because it's oblique — no one says 'Scooby-Doo,' so it rewards the audience for getting it. Jeff's casualness sells the absurdity. Well above average for a throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I am not saying 'bong.' That is a drug word and I don't say drug words.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You can't make me say 'bong.'

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I will not say 'bong,' 'bong,' 'bong,' 'bong,' 'bong.'

jokes.text: Are you sure that my costume was on backwards? Somehow, I felt more confident before.
jokes.setup: Britta is told her costume was on backwards
jokes.punchline: She says she felt MORE confident wearing it wrong — implying the front is somehow more exposing or awkward
jokes.explanation: Modest Britta character beat — her obliviousness about her costume combined with backfiring self-awareness is consistent with her character. Decent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's completely inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Thank you!

jokes.text: I don't think my character would say 'tripping balls.' That's not a question. I don't think my character would say 'tripping balls,' okay?
jokes.setup: Troy prefaces his complaint with 'I have a question,' then Annie points out it's not a question, then he repeats the complaint identically
jokes.punchline: The wordless repetition after being corrected is the joke — he has no alternative response, just re-states the same objection
jokes.explanation: Classic Troy construction — the repeated beat after the correction is perfectly economical. The structure (setup → subversion → identical repetition as non-answer) is tight. Troy's earnest dignity clashing with the phrase 'tripping balls' is the core of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Ding-dong!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Dean-dong!

jokes.text: I wish I had seen a show like this. Might have helped me avoid mistakes.
jokes.setup: The group discusses the value of drug education shows
jokes.punchline: Abed delivers this in a confessional talking head — his life 'mistakes' are hilariously mysterious coming from him, but he delivers it with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Works primarily on Abed's delivery and enigmatic character — the audience imagines whatever 'mistakes' means for Abed, which is funnier than any specific answer.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Charleston Chews are a gateway candy. I've seen it happen. First it's just one Charleston Chew, then it's two, then suddenly you're mainlining Whoppers like some kind of candy fiend.

jokes.text: My school had plenty of shows like this and I think sitting through them drove me to drugs.
jokes.setup: Characters express support for drug education shows
jokes.punchline: Britta undercuts the premise by suggesting drug education shows create drug users — a genuine sociological critique delivered as a casual aside
jokes.explanation: Sharp Britta line — it's both a real critique and a self-own (she's admitting she did drugs). Perfectly in character for the performative contrarian who undermines good intentions. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I would love to help, but I have a very important hotel visit this weekend. I need to break in my new chambermaid outfit.

jokes.text: You don't respond to anything appropriately. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Annie scolds Britta for her contrary response
jokes.punchline: Britta takes 'you don't respond appropriately' as a compliment and says 'thank you'
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat exchange — the punchline IS the inappropriate response, which proves Annie's point in real-time. Structurally elegant and utterly Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, where's the Dean going in that bee costume? He's supposed to be the front singer of the bee band!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I guess you could say he's really... bee-ing a solo act now.

jokes.text: Dean dong. Heh, heh, heh.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton arrives and announces himself
jokes.punchline: He calls himself 'Dean dong' instead of 'ding dong' — a phallic self-pun he clearly finds hilarious
jokes.explanation: Very Dean Pelton — the pun itself is weak but his obvious delight in it is the character joke. The 'heh heh heh' laugh is part of the bit, suggesting he planned this. Running gag potential for the series.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: If a bee is flying away from you, is it leaving, or are you leaving it?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Relative to the ground, you're both stationary and moving simultaneously.

jokes.text: With any luck, we'll get rid of all those Charleston Chews in the vending machines.
jokes.setup: Dean is enthusiastic about the drug awareness show helping at-risk kids
jokes.punchline: His actual motivation is revealed to be clearing out vending machine inventory — an absurdly petty institutional concern grafted onto noble rhetoric
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Dean Pelton — noble cause immediately undercut by institutional triviality. The specificity of 'Charleston Chews' makes it funnier than a generic candy. Becomes a callback payoff later.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not saying texting is bad. I'm saying text flirting is bad. It's like electricity—sure, we need it to survive, but nobody's falling in love with their power bill.

jokes.text: Oh, I would love to, Annie. But as you can see from my outfit, I have plans. So off to the airport Ramada.
jokes.setup: Annie asks if Dean wants to participate in the drug show; he's wearing an unexplained themed outfit
jokes.punchline: He's dressed for something happening at an 'airport Ramada' — the combination of costume + that specific venue implies a fetish event but nothing is confirmed, just left hanging
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Dean Pelton moment — the joke is entirely in what's NOT said. 'Airport Ramada' is specifically chosen to imply a seedy but enthusiastic subculture gathering. The costume detail audiences can see makes this land bigger live. Dean's breezy non-explanation ('as you can see from my outfit') is perfect economy. Among the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm going to prove I'm the father by doing something bizarrely romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm going to serenade you with an R. Kelly song.

jokes.text: How come he gets a front stinger?
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton leaves in his elaborate costume
jokes.punchline: Pierce watches enviously and asks why the Dean has a 'front stinger' on his bee costume — both a costuming complaint and an inadvertent phallic observation
jokes.explanation: The joke cuts Pierce's jealousy of the Dean down to absurd costume-envy while delivering a great double entendre. Perfectly calibrated — Pierce doesn't know what he's said.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Who? I have no idea who you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, him! Yeah, he's terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, who?

jokes.text: That's like saying you don't work by electric light. You want an active sex life, part of it's texting.
jokes.setup: Britta says she doesn't like flirting by text
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a mock-wisdom comparison between electricity and digital flirting — confident, slightly absurd, and very Jeff Winger
jokes.explanation: Jeff at his pseudo-philosopher best — the electric light analogy is just specific enough to sound convincing and just absurd enough to be funny. Fits his lecturing voice perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I was in a commercial once. Back in the seventies, I did a spot for hemorrhoid cream. They had me compare the before and after to a baby's bottom.

jokes.text: Shirley, since I might be the father of your unborn child, I made you a mix tape.
jokes.setup: Chang approaches Shirley with a gift
jokes.punchline: The monumental gravity of potential paternity is paired with the bathos of a mix tape — specifically an obsolete cassette mix tape
jokes.explanation: Chang's oblivious romanticism is perfectly calibrated — the gravitas of paternity uncertainty paired with a mix tape is a great bathos joke. Escalated further by it being a cassette (anachronistic) with a Craigslist workaround.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Name a country.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Russia.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Russia! Yes, I was just about to say that.

jokes.text: I hope you like Johnny Gill. And since you probably don't have a cassette player, here's a list of used ones on Craigslist.
jokes.setup: Chang gives Shirley a cassette mix tape
jokes.punchline: He anticipated she can't play it and provided a Craigslist list as a workaround — the extra effort makes his obliviousness sweeter and more absurd
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'mix tape' to 'Craigslist cassette player list' is a perfect second beat — it shows Chang thought about this, which makes it both sweeter and more ridiculous. 'Johnny Gill' as the artist choice is inspired specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The message is the star of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What about Jeff? He's pretty prominent.

jokes.text: I don't know who you're talking about. Chang. / I don't know who you're talking about. He doesn't exist.
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Britta she'll have to acknowledge Chang eventually
jokes.punchline: Britta doubles down on denying Chang's existence — the second denial ('He doesn't exist') escalates the first into absurdist magical thinking
jokes.explanation: Good escalation within two beats — first denial is defensive, second denial ('He doesn't exist') is a full commitment to delusion. The structure works.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Hey baby, it's me. I've been thinking about you all day. Why don't you come over tonight and we can finally be alone together?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I want to do things to you that would make your head spin.

jokes.text: Pierce reveals he was the 'Gerber baby of moist towelettes' in Hawthorne Wipes TV commercials in the '50s
jokes.setup: Pierce pulls Annie aside to pitch his acting credentials
jokes.punchline: 'Gerber baby of moist towelettes' — the specificity of this legacy (moist towelettes, not food) and his evident pride in it
jokes.explanation: Superb Pierce backstory — the Hawthorne Wipes empire is an absurd but internally consistent piece of Pierce lore. 'Gerber baby of moist towelettes' is a genuinely great formulation that tells us everything about Pierce's warped self-image in five words.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why would you text her that?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because I'm confident and mysterious.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You just sent her a picture of your foot.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly. Mysterious.

jokes.text: Name any country. Russia. [Pierce does Russian accent]
jokes.setup: Pierce pitches his skills including 'foreign accents' and invites Annie to name a country
jokes.punchline: The gag is entirely in what happens — a Pierce Hawthorne Russian accent, which the audience can safely assume is horrifying
jokes.explanation: The joke lives entirely in Chevy Chase's performance, which the transcript can only imply. As a visual/performance gag it likely lands well; as text it's setup without punchline. Rewatch value because the accent itself is the content.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: There's a dangerous person in the hallway. You might want to stay in here.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's just my landlord. He's intimidating, but he's not dangerous.

jokes.text: Do you know what I think is really great about this show? The only real star of it is the message. / Right, of course. Is the message Jeff Winger? He's on every page of this thing.
jokes.setup: Annie tries to diplomatically redirect Pierce's ego away from the show
jokes.punchline: Pierce immediately identifies 'the message' as a synonym for Jeff, revealing he's jealous of Jeff and believes the show revolves around starring roles
jokes.explanation: Annie's diplomatic redirection and Pierce's instant bypass of it is tight construction. 'Is the message Jeff Winger?' is a great line — Pierce interprets every abstraction as a competition for screen time.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, you're living above a sex shop? That's... that's actually pretty cool. So are they expanding? Because I've got some capital I'm looking to invest.

jokes.text: Oh. It's from Marcus. 'I'll be at the show tomorrow night. Can't wait to see you. Are you really wearing a cat costume?'
jokes.setup: Jeff finds Britta's phone and reads an incoming text from 'Marcus'
jokes.punchline: The flirtatious cat costume question from 'Marcus' sets up a misunderstanding — the audience suspects something before Jeff does
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the episode's B-plot — the comedy here is structural (dramatic irony building). Weak in isolation but crucial as a foundation. Rewatch value as the first domino.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, you're telling me you can't afford a house? But what about your trust fund?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't have a trust fund, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, what about your parents' house? Can't you just... live there?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: They want me to be independent.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Independent? That's adorable. You know what I did when I was your age? I bought three houses. Just for fun. Didn't even live in them.

jokes.text: Well, Marcus, you are in luck. / What are you doing? / Dragging Britta kicking and screaming into 1997.
jokes.setup: Jeff decides to respond to 'Marcus' on Britta's behalf to help her flirt
jokes.punchline: 'Dragging Britta kicking and screaming into 1997' — 1997 specifically (not the present) implies Britta is so behind that even getting to 1997 is an achievement
jokes.explanation: Genuinely quotable. The specificity of '1997' (not 2010, the present) is a perfect character insult — it implies Britta is so technologically behind that even reaching 1997 would be an upgrade. Economy and character integration are excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm saving up for a new laptop with my Period Fairy money.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Period Fairy? What the hell is that?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know, the Period Fairy. She comes when you get your period and leaves you money under your pillow.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's not a thing.

jokes.text: 'There's not much to the cat costume. But can't wait to show you what's underneath.'
jokes.setup: Jeff texts a flirtatious message to 'Marcus' on Britta's behalf, not knowing Marcus is her teenage nephew
jokes.punchline: The text itself is innocent flirtation — but dramatic irony makes it deeply inappropriate, all landing harder when the reveal comes
jokes.explanation: Dramatic irony engine — the audience suspects the problem before the characters do, making the text funnier in retrospect. Good construction even if the text itself isn't exceptionally crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The Period Fairy is a magical creature who comes when you get your period and leaves you money under your pillow.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Is she hot?

jokes.text: Dragging Britta kicking and screaming into 1997.
jokes.setup: Abed asks what Jeff is doing by texting on Britta's phone.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's framing of text flirtation as futuristic ('dragging into 1997') is self-aware about how dated the premise is — but he delivers it with complete confidence anyway.
jokes.explanation: The specific year '1997' is the joke — not 'the future' or 'the present,' but a specific, slightly past year that acknowledges text flirting is long-established, making Jeff seem even more pompous for acting like he's doing something cutting-edge. Economical and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, this apartment reminds me of my first place. Roaches big enough to file taxes, a bathtub that doubled as a science experiment, but it had character.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That sounds horrible.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Horrible? It was magical. Don't you ever want to live somewhere that builds character?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: How could you think that's a good idea? / I got a better question. How could it not be a great idea?
jokes.setup: Abed questions Jeff's decision to send flirtatious texts from Britta's phone
jokes.punchline: Jeff reframes the question from 'good idea' to 'great idea' — the escalation in self-confidence despite the obvious wrong he's doing is pure Jeff Winger
jokes.explanation: Jeff's rhetorical sleight-of-hand — upgrading 'good' to 'great' as a deflection — is a great character bit. It's exactly how Jeff operates: winning arguments by reframing them.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm going to make it rain on you people.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And by 'make it rain,' I mean I'm literally going to throw dollar bills in the air.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's the most dignified way to give money.

jokes.text: Pierce, what are you doing here? / Never mind that. There's a rapist in the hallway. / That's my landlord. And if he wanted to rape you, you'd be raped.
jokes.setup: Pierce has followed Annie home and announces danger in her hallway
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat correction and her confident assessment of her landlord's restraint ('you'd be raped') is shockingly blunt and reveals Pierce's paranoia while normalizing a rough neighborhood
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in Annie's matter-of-fact assessment of her neighborhood — 'you'd be raped' as reassurance is darkly funny and tells us volumes about how normalized the danger is for her. Dark but earned through character logic.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I've been selling my eggs for money.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's smart. You should save some for later. You never know when you'll need eggs.

jokes.text: Let me answer your question with two of my own. What are you doing in an apartment above Dildopolis? And when did they open a second location?
jokes.setup: Annie asks Pierce why he followed her; he deflects with two questions
jokes.punchline: His second question ('when did they open a second location?') implies he's a Dildopolis regular — the reveal is in his genuine curiosity about the chain's expansion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is elegant: two questions where the first is the expected one and the second is the reveal. 'When did they open a second location?' recontextualizes everything — Pierce is a Dildopolis patron, not a scandalized observer. The misdirection (he seems to be judging Annie) is completely subverted. Economy is excellent, character integration perfect (only Pierce). Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My father always said, 'Son, a man's gotta stay fresh.' That's why he invented Hawthorne Wipes. The only wet wipe that fights bacteria, odor, and the crushing disappointment of not being your father.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I was born in a small town with big dreams. My mother left me at a Denny's. My father found me in the parking lot, wiped me down with a cloth, and said, 'This is your legacy, boy.'

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Hawthorne Wipes: Because some stains are physical, and some stains are emotional.

jokes.text: I don't get it. Aren't everyone's parents rich?
jokes.setup: Annie explains she lives above Dildopolis because she's estranged from her wealthy parents
jokes.punchline: Pierce genuinely cannot process economic stratification outside the wealthy — asking if everyone's parents are rich with sincere bafflement
jokes.explanation: Perfect Pierce obliviousness — his class bubble is so complete that poverty is literally not in his mental model. Delivered as genuine curiosity rather than condescension, which is funnier and more damning.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Dad, I want to be in commercials!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce's Father
dialogue.line: No son of mine is going to be in commercials. You're going to work in the family business.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: But Dad, I have a real shot at this!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce's Father
dialogue.line: The answer is no. And that's final.

jokes.text: Every dollar from the period fairy when I was a kid. / Excuse me, what's a period fairy?
jokes.setup: Annie lists her childhood savings sources; mentions the 'period fairy'
jokes.punchline: Pierce's innocent confusion — he genuinely doesn't know this family tradition exists, making his follow-up question both oblivious and funny
jokes.explanation: Smart setup — 'period fairy' sounds made-up but Annie treats it as obvious, so when Pierce asks, the audience isn't sure who's wrong. Plays on the audience's own uncertainty.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My father was in a commercial once. He played the Dad.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: He was so warm and caring to that little boy in the commercial.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Then he came home and didn't say a word to me for three days.

jokes.text: The fairy that gives you a dollar every time you get your period. / Does she still come?
jokes.setup: Annie explains the period fairy tradition matter-of-factly
jokes.punchline: Pierce's follow-up — 'Does she still come?' — is genuinely ambiguous between sweet naivety (tooth-fairy logic) and uncomfortable overfamiliarity. Either way it's wrong.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — four words, maximum discomfort. The joke works on multiple levels: Pierce might be applying tooth-fairy logic (sweet, stupid), or asking about Annies menstrual cycle (creepy). The ambiguity of which one Pierce means is itself the joke, and the ambiguity is intentional. Among the episode's best crafted exchanges.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, why does he have Whiteout? Doesn't everyone use computers now?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Does she still come?'
jokes.setup: Annie explains the period fairy gives you a dollar when you get your period
jokes.punchline: Pierce's immediate, sincere follow-up question — asking about the fairy's current operational status — is simultaneously innocent and inappropriate
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke with the period fairy setup. The genius is that Pierce's question is both completely sincere AND inadvertently loaded. He just wants to know if the fairy is still operational — there's no intended lewdness — but the phrasing makes it ambiguous enough to get a big reaction. 'Pierce.' as the response is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Zabba-da-zooey!

jokes.text: Annie's reaction beat — 'Pierce.' (name as full sentence)
jokes.setup: Pierce asks 'Does she still come?' about the period fairy
jokes.punchline: Annie's single-word response — his name, delivered as a full stop — is the perfect straight-man beat
jokes.explanation: One-word straight-man beat that lands because of what preceded it. Economy score is 10 because nothing else could be said here. The name as a full sentence is a sitcom staple but executed perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Break a leg! No wait, that's not right. Bee a leg!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Because bees have legs. Six of them. It's more specific encouragement.

jokes.text: You know, you and I are very much alike, Annie. We're both realists. We're both cute.
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to bond with Annie by listing their similarities
jokes.punchline: He includes 'we're both cute' in a list of serious character traits — the self-compliment embedded in an apparent compliment to Annie is both vain and slightly inappropriate
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — genuine affection expressed through oblivious self-centering. 'We're both cute' lands because he's both complimenting her and complimenting himself simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Whose pen is this?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's mine.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I bought it for you.

jokes.text: I found the drapes in a dumpster. / Can you believe it? / Yes.
jokes.setup: Annie shows off her meager apartment; says she found her drapes in a dumpster
jokes.punchline: Pierce's flat 'Yes' — no hesitation, no diplomacy. He completely believes it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic beat — the expectation is that Pierce (a wealthy man) would be politely surprised. His instant 'Yes' is funnier because it doesn't even attempt kindness. Economy near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What if we just gave away the baseballs as part of a drug-free initiative?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, that's just baseballs.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Exactly! Or we could tell people that holding a baseball is just like doing drugs, so they don't need to do drugs anymore.

jokes.text: It's not mine. It's yours. You've earned it for being strong. It's going to drop into your hands from out of nowhere... because I was never here.
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to give Annie money; she refuses; he insists
jokes.punchline: His elaborate framing of the gift as 'from out of nowhere' and 'I was never here' — an unnecessary and badly executed cover story that makes his kindness weirder
jokes.explanation: Pierce's attempt at anonymity while standing in front of Annie is funny — the 'I was never here' line delivered in person makes no logical sense but is perfectly in character for Pierce's self-mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: My nephew just started texting me out of nowhere. He's so interested in me all of a sudden. He keeps asking me to send him pictures, saying he misses seeing me in my old outfits...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, that's... that's not what he means.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What do you mean? He's being so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, he's being a creepy teenage boy.

jokes.text: I'm only taking this because I'm worried about making rent and the procedure for selling eggs takes weeks.
jokes.setup: Annie resists Pierce's money but eventually accepts it
jokes.punchline: She explains her contingency plan was selling her eggs — a surprisingly dark financial reality delivered in a matter-of-fact tone that underscores how dire her situation is
jokes.explanation: Annie's matter-of-fact mention of egg selling is a great dark joke — it reveals the genuine bleakness of her situation while the bureaucratic 'it takes weeks' makes it funnier. Very Annie: even her crisis planning is organized.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I just realized I sent that text to the wrong person!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, you sent a peach and an eggplant emoji to Dean Pelton.

jokes.text: Oh, it was nothing. It seems sort of pointless now. I guess it was to talk about the play.
jokes.setup: Annie asks why Pierce followed her home
jokes.punchline: His admission that he followed her to complain about the play — now that he's given her money, the original purpose is deflated
jokes.explanation: Modest payoff to the stalking setup. Works as a character beat showing Pierce's unexpected softening. Not a standout joke but serves the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed? Abed! Come on, man, I need you right now. This is serious.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Fine. FINE. You know what? I don't need you. I'll just figure this out myself like I always do.

jokes.text: And who cares if I don't have any lines? ... 'Don't call me honey, honey'? Yeah, that's it, you should do that.
jokes.setup: Pierce has a moment of genuine humility about his role; Annie encourages him
jokes.punchline: Annie validates Pierce by encouraging his improvised line — the callback to the earlier 'Don't call me honey, honey' recontextualizes it as the defining Pierce moment
jokes.explanation: Effective callback that also does emotional work — Annie's encouragement of Pierce feels genuine, and 'Don't call me honey, honey' is now their shared moment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: ...That's it?

jokes.text: Pierce re-enacts Hawthorne Wipes commercial — 'Hello, I'm Cornelius Hawthorne... when I discovered the cleansing power of moist cotton fresh from the field. Isn't that right, son?'
jokes.setup: Pierce demonstrates his acting experience by performing from an old Hawthorne Wipes commercial
jokes.punchline: The commercial itself — portentous voice, pioneer mythology ('fresh from the field'), asking an invisible 'son' — is a parody of pompous brand advertising
jokes.explanation: Performance-dependent joke — Chevy Chase doing a pompous patriarch voice for a moist towelette commercial is funnier in execution than on paper. The lore expansion of the Hawthorne empire is good world-building comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Why does everyone ignore me? Is it because I'm Asian?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No, Chang, it's because you're weird.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, which kind of Asian am I being ignored for?

jokes.text: Pierce re-enacts being a child in the commercial and his father rejecting him: 'Well, then you should've done better in your damn audition.'
jokes.setup: Pierce performs the commercial; his child self asks to be in it too; the father character refuses
jokes.punchline: Pierce is re-enacting his own childhood rejection — by his own father, in a moist towelette commercial. The darkness of this landing mid-performance is both funny and sad.
jokes.explanation: Surprisingly resonant — Pierce roleplaying both his cold father AND his rejected child self explains his entire ego in one bit. 'Your damn audition' for a moist towelette commercial is a devastating small detail. The darkness is earned because Pierce delivers it straight; he's not joking about the wound. This is Community's signature move: wrapping pathos in absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Because you're a sociopath, Chang. We all know it. We've all accepted it. But you keep doing crazy stuff and expecting us to act surprised, like we don't already know you're insane.

jokes.text: What's your name, son? / Nigel. / You're a good boy, Nigel. Your father is a lucky man.
jokes.setup: In his commercial re-enactment, Pierce's father character meets another boy named Nigel
jokes.punchline: Pierce (as his father) lavishes praise on 'Nigel' — a stranger's child — immediately after rejecting Pierce himself. The praise for Nigel is a direct contrast to Pierce's own rejection.
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best — Pierce voicing his father's warmth toward a stranger's son ('Your father is a lucky man') after his own rejection is a compact portrait of childhood neglect turned into comedy. The name 'Nigel' is perfect specificity. This is Community firing on all cylinders — joke, character depth, and pathos simultaneously. The rewatch bonus is for catching that Pierce never stopped auditioning for his father's approval.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Is it wrong that I'm getting aroused right now?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: Okay, guys, remember, the most important thing is to have fun. The second is to know all your lines and not mess up a thing. Actually, flip those.
jokes.setup: Annie gives her pre-show pep talk prioritizing 'fun'
jokes.punchline: 'Actually, flip those' — she immediately overrides her own encouragement, revealing that her real priority is perfection
jokes.explanation: Economical and highly character-specific — this is Annie Edison in two beats. She knows the 'right' thing to say, says it, then immediately can't sustain the lie. 'Flip those' is quotable and perfectly captures her anxiety.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm feeling pretty blue in this green costume.

jokes.text: Hey, Crayon, do you know where I can get some drugs? I need them. / Unfortunately, you can get them anywhere. / Anywhere? / I'm here. / Zabadazooey.
jokes.setup: Pierce demonstrates his revised script additions, including the new 'Drugs' entrance
jokes.punchline: 'Zabadazooey' — Pierce's invented catchphrase for Drugs, nonsensical and self-satisfied
jokes.explanation: Pierce's invented word 'zabadazooey' is a great absurdist creation — it sounds like something an elderly man would think is what 'the kids' find cool. The deadpan approval from Jeff and Troy that follows sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, what are you supposed to be?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm Mewtwo, the most powerful Pokémon ever created.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pierce, you're just wearing a lab coat and a weird helmet.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Exactly. Now watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Mewtwo, Mewtwo, Mewtwo! I am the clone, the chosen one!

jokes.text: Break a stinger. / For the bees.
jokes.setup: Jeff gives a 'break a leg' theater send-off
jokes.punchline: 'Break a stinger' — the bee-specific version of the theater phrase, with Annie solemnly clarifying 'For the bees'
jokes.explanation: Clean wordplay with good structure — 'Break a stinger' works as both theater tradition and costume-specific logic. 'For the bees' as solemn clarification is a nice extra beat.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm back! Did you miss me?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, this is a funeral.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know, I know. But I'm alive! Unlike the guy in the box.

jokes.text: Annie, uh, I don't feel comfortable with the 'zabadazooey' line. / The one you wrote? / I got it. Let's give Jeff the zabadazooey line and I'll come in with 'good one.'
jokes.setup: Troy objects to the zabadazooey line; Annie reminds him Pierce wrote it
jokes.punchline: Pierce instantly offers to give Jeff his precious 'zabadazooey' line and take the smaller 'good one' — but his reasoning is about ego management, not generosity
jokes.explanation: Pierce's willingness to sacrifice 'zabadazooey' as a power move is good — he's playing the long game. The callback structure works.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I didn't get flushed. I got stuck behind the toilet. There's a whole ecosystem back there. I'm telling you, I saw things that would make you question everything.

jokes.text: By the way, is this your pen? I think I put it back in my pocket after I wrote you that check yesterday.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to run rehearsal; Pierce casually outs the secret money arrangement in front of everyone
jokes.punchline: Pierce sabotages Annie's secret by mentioning the check in public while pretending it's just about a pen — his social obliviousness destroys her credibility
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — the secret is revealed through pure obliviousness rather than malice. The triviality of 'is this your pen' as the vehicle for a bombshell revelation is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, you know, I did pay for your textbooks last semester.

jokes.text: Also, I think it'd be better for my character if I wear his leather jacket.
jokes.setup: Pierce has already been pushing script changes; now wants Jeff's costume piece too
jokes.punchline: He wants Jeff's leather jacket for the character Drugs — another territorial ego move that continues his escalating takeover of the show
jokes.explanation: Part of a consistent escalation of Pierce's demands. Not a standout joke but serves the building comedic pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, I have an idea!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Bee-lieve in me!

jokes.text: You can't ignore me forever. ... Okay, you probably can.
jokes.setup: Chang approaches Shirley backstage; she ignores him
jokes.punchline: Chang's confident declaration immediately collapses into self-doubt: 'Okay, you probably can.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat structure. The collapse from 'you can't' to 'you probably can' is timed flawlessly and reveals Chang's complete lack of leverage. The self-awareness without behavioral change is a great character note. Economical and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Drugs! Drugs! Drugs!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, you want Drugs? I'll give you Drugs. I AM Drugs! I always have been. When I was a kid, my father told me, 'Pierce, you're gonna be somebody.' And I said, 'Dad, I'm already Drugs.'

jokes.text: My nephew Marcus actually goes to San Ramon Middle School. He texted me: 'You are the coolest aunt in the world.'
jokes.setup: Britta reveals 'Marcus' is her 14-year-old nephew — the person Jeff sent the flirty texts to
jokes.punchline: Dramatic irony — audience knows what 'Marcus' sent back; Britta is reading a completely different message (the original one before Jeff's interference)
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands — this is the moment the B-plot detonates. The gap between Britta's pride ('coolest aunt') and what Jeff has done creates maximum cringe setup. Well-structured irony.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, you're not withdrawing your support. You're just finally showing your true colors. And honestly? We all knew they were there.

jokes.text: What does this mean? It's eight, an equal sign and a greater than symbol? / Let me see. You better get changed.
jokes.setup: Britta shows Jeff the 'emotipenis' Marcus sent back
jokes.punchline: Jeff recognizes it instantly, diverts Britta, and takes her phone — his guilt and panic expressed through rapid misdirection
jokes.explanation: Good payoff beat — Britta's genuine confusion ('eight, an equal sign...') is a great character detail (she's both internet-unsavvy and literal). Jeff's instant recognition is played through panic rather than exposition.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done. This friendship is over.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And another thing - I'm taking back all the friendly advice I've given you. Especially that tip about the store downstairs from Annie's apartment.

jokes.text: Abed, we screwed up. You know that text we sent? It was to Britta's nephew. He sent her an emotipenis.
jokes.setup: Jeff confesses to Abed that the flirtatious text went to Britta's 14-year-old nephew
jokes.punchline: 'He sent her an emotipenis' — the coinage 'emotipenis' is both a perfect new word and immediately clear
jokes.explanation: 'Emotipenis' is an outstanding coinage — instantly understood, perfectly describes the emoji representation, and funnier than any explicit description could be. High quotability. The word is so good it elevates the whole scene. Among the episode's best individual lines for pure craft of invention.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Clinical description of absurd crisis

jokes.text: Marcus responds: 'You called me by name. It wasn't a mistake. Don't be afraid.'
jokes.setup: Jeff texts Marcus pretending to be Britta, claiming it was a mistake
jokes.punchline: Marcus's response is seductive teen-movie dialogue — 'Don't be afraid' — which is both hilariously confident for a 14-year-old and deeply wrong
jokes.explanation: The 14-year-old's confident seduction lines read as a parody of teen romantic movies — 'Don't be afraid' is exactly what a teenager thinks is smooth. The escalation of his confidence despite the situation makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We need someone crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Did you say you need someone to organize your files?

jokes.text: I was drunk. We can't do this. / I'm drunk too. On lust.
jokes.setup: Jeff (as Britta) tries to shut down the conversation by claiming drunkenness
jokes.punchline: 'I'm drunk too. On lust.' — Marcus's reply is a spectacular teenage cliché delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'Drunk on lust' is a legendary bad-teen-romance line. It's the perfect peak of the escalating text exchange — it's exactly what a 14-year-old who's read too many romance novels would write. Exquisitely quotable. Near-perfect economy (four words). The reactions from Jeff and Abed ('There's a picture. / Oh. That's disappointing. / Wow. Who does that?') extend the joke perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You better watch yourself, or I'm gonna come to your school and... and I'm gonna eat all your cupcakes at the bake sale!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Then I'm gonna show up at your birthday party and... and I'm gonna tell everyone your real age!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And then I'm gonna find out where you live and... and replace all your Halloween candy with healthy alternatives!

jokes.text: There's a picture. / Oh. That's disappointing. / Wow. Who does that?
jokes.setup: Marcus texts back a photo in response to Jeff's 'drunk' text
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Abed's layered reactions — 'That's disappointing' implies the picture is underwhelming, 'Who does that?' expresses moral outrage while implying Jeff knows exactly who does that
jokes.explanation: Three-reaction cascade perfectly staged: Jeff identifies the picture, Abed evaluates it aesthetically ('disappointing'), Jeff performs outrage while implying familiarity. Each beat is funnier than the last. 'That's disappointing' from Abed is a perfect Abed reaction — evaluating the technical execution of the picture.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You think you can hurt me? I've been through worse! I'm Chang! I'm a black belt! I'm—OW! OW! Stop it! STOP IT!

jokes.text: Are you ignoring me because I'm Korean? / You're Chinese. / Oh, there's a difference?
jokes.setup: Chang tries to get Shirley to acknowledge him; accuses her of racial bias
jokes.punchline: Shirley corrects his nationality; Chang questions whether the difference matters — using his own ethnicity as a rhetorical weapon while getting it wrong
jokes.explanation: Chang doesn't even know his own nationality correctly — which completely deflates his racial grievance claim. This is very specific to Chang: he's not just wrong, he's wrong about himself. 'Oh, there's a difference?' as a follow-up is shameless and funny. Highly quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You started this whole thing by texting me at 2 AM!

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.line: I was concerned about you! And you responded!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because I thought you were dying!

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.line: Well, I'm the one who's actually hurt here.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you're the victim? You're the one who sent me those messages!

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.line: I was vulnerable, Jeff. I needed someone to talk to.

jokes.text: It's because you're crazy. There's something wrong with you. And the idea that I was with you means there's something wrong with me.
jokes.setup: Shirley finally addresses Chang directly
jokes.punchline: Her self-indictment ('there's something wrong with me') — she's angrier at herself than at Chang, which is both funny and sad
jokes.explanation: More dramatic than comedic, but Shirley's self-directed anger provides enough irony to qualify. The escalation from 'you're crazy' to 'I'm also crazy for being with you' is good character construction.

jokes.text: Shirley, funeral.
jokes.setup: Shirley is telling Chang off with emotional intensity backstage
jokes.punchline: Jeff interrupts with the single word 'funeral' — their cue to get on stage for the funeral scene
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation — the interruption of Shirley's heartfelt speech with the mundane 'funeral' as a stage direction is a great beat. Maximum economy (one word). The incongruity of 'funeral' as a cue during an argument about paternity is a nice bit of dark absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You didn't know I wasn't your aunt?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.line: I don't get out much.

jokes.text: Well, that answers my question. Jeff Winger is sexy even in a coffin.
jokes.setup: Jeff appears on stage in a coffin (the bee funeral scene)
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately shifts from emotional crisis mode to admiring Jeff in a coffin — the tonal whiplash is the joke, plus the specificity of the coffin as a lust context
jokes.explanation: Good Shirley moment — her attraction to Jeff being so powerful it overrides both her crisis and basic context ('even in a coffin') is funny and in character. The tonal shift from crisis to appreciation is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh, I'd be happy to help arrange that. I could set up a meeting between you and yourself. We could rent out the cafeteria, get some name tags, maybe you two could finally get to know each other.

jokes.text: I was looking for a lighter. / What are you wearing? This is a funeral. / I got this, Annie.
jokes.setup: Pierce arrives late to the stage carrying something and wearing an unexpected costume
jokes.punchline: Pierce's casual deflection ('I got this, Annie') after both breaking character and apparently costuming himself wrong
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for Pierce's scene disruption. Rewatch value because knowing what he's about to do makes the deflection funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Thank you, thank you. I appreciate the recognition.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You were amazing out there, Chang!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, I did study the craft. My acting coach said I really captured the essence of a deranged lunatic terrorizing children.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... that's not actually a compliment.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: In the improv community, we call that range.

jokes.text: I can't believe Fluffy's dead. I know I'm green, but I feel blue.
jokes.setup: Pierce plays his bee character at the funeral scene
jokes.punchline: 'I know I'm green, but I feel blue' — a bee/color pun that makes no sense for the bee character (bees aren't green) but sounds like the kind of pun Pierce would be proud of
jokes.explanation: Modest Pierce pun — the green/blue color wordplay is typically bad but that's the point. 'I know I'm green' is especially nonsensical for a bee, which is characteristically oblivious Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Group hug! Everyone together now, we've all learned something today.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Just like when I told Jeff in private about my feelings, and he said—well, he said some things we agreed to never repeat.

jokes.text: Look, it's Drugs with a crazy wig and sparklers.
jokes.setup: Pierce is supposed to get flushed down a toilet in the next scene
jokes.punchline: Instead he returns with a 'crazy wig and sparklers' — a maximally Pierce interpretation of making a dramatic entrance
jokes.explanation: Visual gag that works because it's described in dialogue — 'crazy wig and sparklers' as Pierce's idea of cool Drugs iconography tells us everything. Performance-dependent but the description lands.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Before you say anything, Annie, I want you to know that I did nothing wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: But here's $200.

jokes.text: Pokémon!
jokes.setup: Pierce enters as Drugs with sparklers and a wig
jokes.punchline: A child shouts 'Pokémon!' — completely misidentifying Drugs, which both undermines Pierce's intended cool entrance and reveals what actually resonates with children
jokes.explanation: One word, maximum comedy. The child identifying Pierce's drug character as a Pokémon is a perfect joke — it's exactly what a child would say, it completely deflates Pierce, and it accidentally reveals why Pierce's character design works on 10-year-olds. Economical and genuinely funny. Great meta-commentary on drug education show aesthetics.

dialogue.speaker: Advertisement
dialogue.line: Are you tired of missing out on amazing deals? Well, stay up late with us! We're having a midnight madness sale at Adult Emporium!

dialogue.speaker: Advertisement
dialogue.line: Everything must go! Fifty percent off select items, buy one get one free on certain products, and free shipping on orders over fifty dollars!

dialogue.speaker: Advertisement
dialogue.line: That's right folks, we're open till 2 AM tonight only. Come on down to Adult Emporium, where we take care of your... late night needs.

dialogue.speaker: Advertisement
dialogue.line: Adult Emporium. We're more open than you are.

jokes.text: I don't think that's right, Drugs. / Nobody asked you, Crayon.
jokes.setup: Troy tries to correct Pierce's script improvisation as they're on stage
jokes.punchline: 'Nobody asked you, Crayon' — Pierce dismisses Troy by his character name (Crayon), which is both condescending and weirdly accurate to their dynamic
jokes.explanation: Pierce using 'Crayon' as an insult mid-performance is a good bit — it blurs the in-show and real-world dynamics while revealing Pierce's low opinion of Troy. The character name as a dismissal is an efficient construction.

dialogue.speaker: Advertisement
dialogue.line: Discrete billing is just as obvious as original name

jokes.text: Well, I hope you're proud of yourself. Look what you've done. / Oh, yeah? Well, look what I'm doing now.
jokes.setup: Troy tries to shame Pierce's Drugs character for corrupting the bee
jokes.punchline: Pierce's Drugs character responds by doubling down — 'look what I'm doing now' implies a further escalation on stage that the kids respond to
jokes.explanation: Setup beat for the kids' positive reaction to Pierce's Drugs character. The escalation is building but this specific exchange is the weakest part of the sequence.

jokes.text: Should we get the dean, call in a bomb threat? Should we set off the sprinklers? / It's not that big a deal. The kids are into it.
jokes.setup: The group watches Pierce's Drugs character becoming increasingly popular with the kids
jokes.punchline: Jeff's completely calm 'the kids are into it' as a reason not to intervene on a drug character who's become an idol to at-risk children
jokes.explanation: Jeff's pragmatist nihilism is a good character beat — 'the kids are into it' as a sufficient justification for a pro-drugs stage show is absurdist in the best Jeff way. Britta's bomb-threat solution is good escalation.

jokes.text: Being flushed doesn't mean you're dead. I could be a floater.
jokes.setup: Annie tells Pierce that the show is over, his character was flushed
jokes.punchline: Pierce invents toilet-based narrative logic to justify continuing — 'a floater' as a dramatic arc
jokes.explanation: Pierce deploying actual fecal knowledge ('a floater') as a dramatic comeback is a great absurdist escalation. The confidence with which he presents toilet mechanics as narrative logic is pure Pierce. 'I could be a floater' deserves to be a standalone quote.

jokes.text: A floater is when you have a number two... / I know what a floater is, Pierce.
jokes.setup: Pierce explains the term 'floater' to Annie as if she doesn't know
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat 'I know what a floater is, Pierce' — the exasperation of having to establish that she understands toilet terminology
jokes.explanation: Annie's dignified refusal to have a bowel movement explained to her is a good reaction beat. The pairing of Annie's propriety and Pierce's casual scatology is reliably funny.

jokes.text: It just wouldn't make any sense in the flow of the show.
jokes.setup: Annie tells Pierce that a 'floater' returning doesn't work narratively
jokes.punchline: Annie says 'flow of the show' — inadvertently using toilet imagery in her anti-floater argument
jokes.explanation: Nice accidental wordplay — Annie uses 'flow' while arguing against Pierce's floater logic, apparently unaware. The unintentional pun is funnier than an intentional one would be.

jokes.text: Bzzz. Getting rid of Drugs was a great 'ibee-a.' I'm flying higher than I ever have, thanks to not Drugs.
jokes.setup: The original show continues despite Pierce's interruptions; Shirley delivers her lines
jokes.punchline: 'Ibee-a' as the bee-pun version of 'idea' — plus the grammatically awkward 'thanks to not Drugs'
jokes.explanation: In-show anti-drug dialogue joke — the 'ibee-a' pun is the kind of groan-worthy writing that Annie's show would have. The humor is meta: the show within the show has terrible puns, which is the point.

jokes.text: Chuck it at his nuts!
jokes.setup: Pierce's Drugs character has fully won over the children despite the anti-drug message
jokes.punchline: A child shouts 'Chuck it at his nuts!' when the bee tries to banish Drugs — the kids have completely sided with Pierce/Drugs
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the children-love-Drugs arc. The at-risk kids' immediate jump to violence against the anti-drug character is bleakly funny and proves Annie's show has spectacularly backfired. The child's specific instruction ('at his nuts') is unexpected and funnier for the specificity.

jokes.text: Ain't no party without Drugs.
jokes.setup: Pierce has been physically attacked by children throwing baseballs but returns triumphant
jokes.punchline: 'Ain't no party without Drugs' — Pierce/Drugs' motto, which is both the worst possible message for an anti-drug show and genuinely how the kids feel
jokes.explanation: Classic Community irony — the drug character's triumphant catchphrase is exactly the message the show was designed to prevent. Delivered with Pierce's complete obliviousness. Good line.

jokes.text: I love you, Drugs. / Yo, pass it this way. / We want Drugs! We want Drugs!
jokes.setup: The kids have fully turned pro-Drugs after Pierce's performance
jokes.punchline: 'Yo, pass it this way' from a child — a 14-year-old using drug-sharing vernacular at an anti-drug show
jokes.explanation: The 'pass it this way' detail from a child is a great escalation — it suggests the drug metaphor has fully been absorbed as literal. The chanting 'We want Drugs!' is the peak of the anti-drug show's catastrophic failure.

jokes.text: Listen to that, Dad. They're high on me. I'm a god. / Where's that Nigel now?
jokes.setup: Pierce basks in the children's adulation
jokes.punchline: 'Where's that Nigel now?' — a callback to the Hawthorne Wipes commercial scene where his father favored Nigel over Pierce
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best — the callback to 'Nigel' pays off the earlier scene perfectly. Pierce's triumph over Nigel via children chanting for a drug character is a devastating comedy of broken psychology. He's talking to his dead father while dressed as Drugs with a sparkler wig. The character integration is as deep as this show gets. 'Where's that Nigel now?' earns its score as a callback that also functions as pure pathos.

jokes.text: And I haven't even used my penis material yet.
jokes.setup: Pierce is celebrating his success with the children
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he has 'penis material' ready for a children's drug show
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines — 'I haven't even used my penis material yet' is a great threat/boast that tells us everything about Pierce. He came prepared with age-inappropriate content for a middle school drug show. The word 'yet' is the key — it's still coming. Economical, deeply character-specific, and very quotable.

jokes.text: You sick, sick, sad old man.
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to blackmail Annie with the money as leverage to stay in the show
jokes.punchline: Annie's reaction — 'sick, sick, sad' — the triple adjective with 'sad' landing as the final blow rather than something stronger
jokes.explanation: Annie's indictment lands because 'sad' is worse than 'sick' — it removes Pierce's agency and makes him pitiable rather than threatening. Good construction for Annie's moral register.

jokes.text: Next time I'm at Dildopolis, I will not be coming upstairs to say hi.
jokes.setup: Pierce has been fired from the show; delivers his final threat to Annie
jokes.punchline: He calls back Dildopolis while confirming he is a Dildopolis regular — his threat is to withhold neighborhood visits, which is itself its own absurdity
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff — 'next time I'm at Dildopolis' fully confirms what joke #29 implied. His threatened snub ('will not be coming upstairs to say hi') reframes visiting Annie as an incidental courtesy during Dildopolis trips. The indignity of the threat is the joke: he's threatening to stop dropping by on his sex toy shopping trips. Excellent character economy and callback structure.

jokes.text: Here's the situation. We've got 50 at-risk pre-teens armed with baseballs, chanting for drugs, who just spent intermission eating nothing but Charleston Chews.
jokes.setup: The group assesses the catastrophic state of the drug show
jokes.punchline: Jeff's clinical summary landing on 'Charleston Chews' — the Dean's vending machine obsession has inadvertently armed sugar-high at-risk kids with baseballs
jokes.explanation: Superb callback payoff — the Charleston Chews throwaway from Dean Pelton has returned as a plot element. Jeff's summary is a great comedy of escalation: 'armed,' 'chanting,' 'Charleston Chews' building to the least expected conclusion. The callback lands perfectly because it was planted so casually.

jokes.text: Thank God.
jokes.setup: Jeff lists the Charleston Chews as part of the crisis
jokes.punchline: Dean Pelton's 'Thank God' — to him, the vending machine clearing is the silver lining of the entire catastrophe
jokes.explanation: Two words, perfect character expression. Dean Pelton's institutional priorities over human welfare in a moment of crisis is defined entirely by 'Thank God.' The callback to the Charleston Chews setup pays off maximally with minimum words. Among the episode's most economical and character-perfect lines.

jokes.text: We just created 50 potential meth-heads. The least we can do is hit the reset button and get that number down to average.
jokes.setup: Group considers abandoning the situation
jokes.punchline: 'Get that number down to average' — Jeff's moral bar is not 'prevent meth use' but 'return to baseline expected meth use rates'
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff Winger moral calculus — the goal isn't to do good, it's to restore statistical normalcy. 'Get that number down to average' is a perfect formulation of Jeff's pragmatic nihilism. Dark, funny, very quotable, and deeply Jeff.

jokes.text: That's a suicide mission. / Did someone say crazy person? / No. No. / Well, I heard it.
jokes.setup: Jeff calls the plan a 'suicide mission'; Chang overhears
jokes.punchline: Chang mishears 'suicide mission' as 'crazy person' — a self-referential misidentification that he insists on despite correction
jokes.explanation: Chang's self-labeling as a 'crazy person' who shows up when summoned is excellent character comedy. His insistence that he heard it despite correction ('Well, I heard it') is a perfect Chang beat — he identifies with craziness as a brand identity.

jokes.text: Greetings, you little snots.
jokes.setup: Britta takes over as the Drugs character to do damage control
jokes.punchline: Her first line as Drugs is 'you little snots' — Britta's affected counter-culture voice manifesting as hostility toward children
jokes.explanation: Perfect Britta — she's supposed to make drugs scary but begins by being condescending to children. 'You little snots' is a great character expression of Britta's particular brand of patronizing activism.

jokes.text: You're not Drugs. / Oh, but I am. Disappointed? Did you expect me to stay the same forever? Because that's not what Drugs does, baby!
jokes.setup: Children reject Britta's version of Drugs compared to Pierce's
jokes.punchline: Britta's Drugs gives a speech about the unexpected nature of drugs — which also works as Britta not understanding what children find fun
jokes.explanation: Britta's Drugs speech about changeability and unpredictability is an inadvertent meta-commentary on actual drug effects, which is funny coming from someone who's supposed to be doing the opposite. 'That's not what Drugs does, baby!' has real Britta energy.

jokes.text: I'm gonna deep-fry your dog and eat your mama's face. And I'm gonna wear your little brother's skin like pajamas.
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to make Drugs seem terrifying to the children
jokes.punchline: Her threats escalate from normal horror ('deep-fry your dog') to surreal body horror ('wear your little brother's skin like pajamas') — Silence of the Lambs energy for 12-year-olds
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sustained jokes. The escalation from 'deep-fry your dog' to 'wear your little brother's skin like pajamas' is a perfect dark comedy progression — each beat more horrifying than the last. The specificity of 'like pajamas' is a great final touch. Britta's earnest commitment to terrorizing children with Silence of the Lambs material is superb character comedy. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: I control your lives and there is nothing you can do.
jokes.setup: Britta continues her Drugs villain speech
jokes.punchline: Accurate description of addiction delivered with Britta's particular brand of heavy-handed messaging
jokes.explanation: Continuation beat after the skin-pajamas peak. Decent escalation but weaker than the surrounding material.

jokes.text: Let's kill him. / Oh, bring it on, Bow Wow.
jokes.setup: Children turn on Britta's scary Drugs character
jokes.punchline: Britta calls the child 'Bow Wow' — a condescending rapper nickname for a child who's about to attack her
jokes.explanation: Britta calling a child 'Bow Wow' is a perfect choice — it's condescending while also aging the character (the reference is a bit dated for 2010, which is very Britta). The beat before she gets attacked is a great reversal of Pierce's triumphant moment.

jokes.text: I gotta tell you, this is the greatest chemical-dependency program I have ever watched. The way you got the kids to think that they needed drugs. And then having them realize that dependence was the enemy. Genius.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton watches the chaos and beats as the show concludes
jokes.punchline: He genuinely believes it was an intentional pedagogical strategy — interpreting the catastrophic accident as sophisticated design
jokes.explanation: Dean Pelton's reading of the accident as genius is a great irony beat — it accidentally validates Community's thesis that chaos can be confused for pedagogy. His breathless praise is a perfect Pelton moment and resolves the episode's central tension with maximum irony.

jokes.text: So now that the show is over, what is the plan for these bee costumes?
jokes.setup: Dean wraps up his praise of the show
jokes.punchline: His immediate pivot to the bee costumes — institutional asset management while children are presumably still sugar-high and traumatized
jokes.explanation: Very Dean Pelton — immediately after praising a traumatizing children's show, his concern is costume inventory. Consistent character logic and a good button to his scene.

jokes.text: Hey, Marcus. I'm Jeff. I'm, like, uh, Britta's boyfriend.
jokes.setup: Jeff approaches Marcus — Britta's 14-year-old nephew — to manage the texting situation
jokes.punchline: 'I'm, like, uh, Britta's boyfriend' — Jeff immediately claims a relationship status that doesn't exist to establish dominance over a 14-year-old
jokes.explanation: Jeff's immediate claim to be Britta's boyfriend as a tactical move against a teenager is a good character beat — he's simultaneously jealous, strategic, and absurdly vain.

jokes.text: It's disgusting, sending those pictures to your aunt. / More disgusting than what you texted to an underage boy? / I didn't know you were you. / I didn't know you weren't my aunt.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts Marcus about the picture he sent
jokes.punchline: The mutual 'I didn't know' — both parties are guilty of the same thing by symmetrical mistake, which makes the moral indignation impossible to maintain
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural symmetry — the mutual 'I didn't know' completely deflates Jeff's moral high ground. The parallel construction ('I didn't know you were you / I didn't know you weren't my aunt') is tight writing. The resolution through mutually assured embarrassment is very funny and structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: Okay. Let's just call this a draw. / Britta doesn't need to ever know about this. / Okay, I'd be happy to, for a price.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Marcus agree to mutual cover-up
jokes.punchline: The 14-year-old immediately pivots to extortion — 'I'd be happy to, for a price'
jokes.explanation: Marcus going full extortionist is a great character reveal — he's apparently a natural schemer. The speed of the pivot from 'mutual understanding' to 'for a price' is very funny.

jokes.text: That was brave of you. I owe you an apology. It was rude to call you crazy. Maybe I haven't been giving you enough credit. / Oh, that's really sweet. Tell you what, why don't I go get Chang, and you can tell him that yourself.
jokes.setup: Shirley apologizes to Britta for calling her crazy; Britta seems touched
jokes.punchline: Britta immediately tries to redirect the apology to Chang — her generosity is strategically aimed at getting out of her own situation
jokes.explanation: Perfect Britta — she doesn't even enjoy the apology before weaponizing it. 'Why don't I go get Chang and you can tell him that yourself' is a great Britta move: deflecting from herself while technically being helpful.

jokes.text: That was brave of you. I owe you an apology... Tell you what, why don't I go get Chang, and you can tell him that yourself.
jokes.setup: Jeff apologizes to Shirley for calling Chang crazy and suggests she tell Chang directly.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's immediate pivot — 'why don't I go get Chang and you can tell him that yourself' — rejects Jeff's apology-by-proxy and forces him into the uncomfortable position of delivering it personally. The joke is on Jeff.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — Jeff's apology meant to smoothly resolve tension instead becomes a trap. Shirley's 'go get Chang and you can tell him that yourself' is a precisely deployed gotcha.

jokes.text: Before you say anything, I want you to know, even though I did nothing wrong, I'm still gonna give you money.
jokes.setup: Pierce approaches Annie after being fired and the whole cast reconciling
jokes.punchline: 'Even though I did nothing wrong, I'm still gonna give you money' — an apology that's also a vindication claim
jokes.explanation: Perfect Pierce apology construction — he leads with innocence, offers money as a gesture, frames it as generosity while maintaining complete denial. 'Even though I did nothing wrong' doing all the character work in five words.

jokes.text: Pierce, I know you don't depend on anyone, but you do depend on people depending on you.
jokes.setup: Annie refuses Pierce's money and explains her reasoning
jokes.punchline: The tongue-twisting psychological insight — 'depend on people depending on you' — delivered by Annie as genuine wisdom
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines — it's a genuine psychological insight about Pierce dressed up as a tongue-twisting line reading. 'You depend on people depending on you' is both funny as a construction and devastating as a character read. This is Community at its best: emotional truth delivered with verbal precision. Annie landing it is perfect character integration — she's the only one who would say it this way.

jokes.text: By the way, you're mom is the period fairy, right?
jokes.setup: Pierce and Annie finish their heart-to-heart; he drops a final question
jokes.punchline: Pierce asking if Annie's mom is the period fairy — bringing back the earlier thread with new context (it was her mom doing it)
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff that reveals Pierce has been thinking about the period fairy this entire time. The question also works as a sweet Pierce moment — he genuinely wants to know. Character and callback working together.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, I found my phone, but has anyone seen my bra?
jokes.setup: Episode seems to be wrapping up with group reconciliation
jokes.punchline: Britta's missing bra — which raises immediate questions about what happened during/after the show, delivered with complete nonchalance
jokes.explanation: Perfect tag ending — the calm delivery of 'has anyone seen my bra?' after a chaotic episode implies far more than it explains. What happened to Britta during the show? The mystery is funnier than any answer. Good economy.

jokes.text: It's 2 a.m., time for Dildopolis' Night Owl Deals.
jokes.setup: Post-credits scene — the episode ends with a Dildopolis store announcement
jokes.punchline: The show ends on an extended Dildopolis ad that runs like a parody of a late-night commercial — 'Night Owl Deals' at a sex toy store
jokes.explanation: Great post-credits joke — the episode that planted Dildopolis as a running gag ends in a full Dildopolis commercial. The deadpan 'Night Owl Deals' and 'we will be closed for Presidents' Day / Just kidding, Dildopolis never closes' are good absurdist details.

jokes.text: Please be advised, we will be closed for Presidents' Day. Just kidding. Dildopolis never closes.
jokes.setup: The Dildopolis PA announcement continues.
jokes.punchline: 'Just kidding. Dildopolis never closes.' — The store's 24/7 operations as a point of pride, delivered with retail announcement formality.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the tag. 'Dildopolis never closes' is an extraordinary sentence delivered with complete retail pride. The setup-reversal structure ('closed for Presidents' Day / just kidding') is well-executed, and 'Dildopolis never closes' as a proud declaration is highly quotable. The commitment to the bit makes it land.

jokes.text: At Dildopolis, your privacy is our top concern. All store purchases will show up on your credit card as ABC Dildos, Incorporated.
jokes.setup: Dildopolis post-credits commercial continues
jokes.punchline: 'ABC Dildos, Incorporated' — the cover name is only marginally more subtle than the actual store name, defeating the purpose of privacy
jokes.explanation: 'ABC Dildos, Incorporated' is a great joke — the privacy cover is so thin it barely qualifies. The gap between 'your privacy is our top concern' and 'ABC Dildos' is perfect irony. Quotable standalone line.

jokes.text: Shopping till you drop? Take a load off at our in-store cafe and enjoy an espresso or our signature cinnamon biscotti.
jokes.setup: Dildopolis commercial ends
jokes.punchline: In-store cafe with 'signature cinnamon biscotti' at a sex toy store — the mundane cafe amenity in this context is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Signature cinnamon biscotti' at Dildopolis is a great absurdist detail — the specificity of a branded baked good at a sex toy store takes the joke further than 'they have a cafe.' Good final button.

tmdb_overview: Pierce's efforts to bribe director Annie may undermine the theater group's antidrug play; Jeff's texting prank puts Britta in an awkward situation.
insight: Drug-comedy premise delivers steady character humor without a single standout laugh.
